rationale: Unauthenticated third-party weather and traffic feeds can be falsified with moderate effort, steering many UAS into unsafe routes or conflicts.
The leak mainly enables future targeted attacks rather than causing direct harm, and it typically needs insider access.
Poisoning the single source of truth spreads simultaneously to every dependent service, so it can corrupt the shared traffic picture across the whole airspace.
Sensor or IMU manipulation can crash individual aircraft, but it usually needs proximity and specialised signal-injection skills.
Phantom tracks injected into tracking, together with masked real conflicts, undermine separation for every aircraft in the monitored volume.
Log tampering happens after the attack and hampers forensics and accountability, but it causes no direct operational harm.
Public regulatory ambiguities need little skill to exploit and weaken the security baseline across USSPs, but they have only indirect safety effects.
Weak identity proofing and stolen credentials are easy to abuse, but each case enables illegitimate flights for a limited set of operators.
The JWT none-algorithm flaw is well known and trivially repeatable once found, and it grants unrestricted flight authorisation.
Deleting no-fly zones through an unsecured API silently opens restricted airspace, including around aerodromes, to every UAS that relies on the database.
Cheap SDR tools make spoofing and jamming of unauthenticated GNSS easy, and the effects cover a whole area and every receiver in it.
Physical sabotage of a vertiport is serious for UAM landings but needs on-site presence and affects a single facility.
Injected geofence data misleads many operators into controlled airspace, but it requires compromising the feed path.
Firmware backdoors give full flight-controller control, but they need physical, production or update-channel access and real expertise.
Tampering with regulator audit records erodes oversight over time, with indirect safety consequences, and needs privileged access.
Vendor-level compromise is hard and stealthy, but it can backdoor the entire deployed fleet at once.
BMS manipulation can force loss of power mid-flight and ground-station outages halt operations, but the scope is mostly local.
Flooding an unprotected gateway is trivial and blocks services for the whole volume, though new authorisations mostly fail safe.
SQL injection on an unpatched database is a commodity attack, and corrupting flight plans as well as exfiltrating them raises the operational risk.
Unencrypted legacy C2 links such as MAVLink are easy to jam or intercept, causing fail-safe crashes, but the effect is limited to the targeted flights.
Stolen API keys allow easy bulk exfiltration of flight plans, which mainly harms confidentiality and could enable later targeting.
